pairs.derivation: Trimalchio's celebrated historical howler: Hannibal at the sack of Troy melting the statues into 'Corinthian' alloy. Anchored to Trimalchio + the named Hannibal; single-name answer supported verbatim; the question's 'perperam' frames it as his claim. The real aetiology (the sack of Corinth) makes the blunder the famous point.

pairs.source_text: Diomedes et Ganymedes duo fratres fuerunt. Horum soror erat Helena. Agamemnon illam rapuit et Dianae cervam subiecit.
pairs.question: Quorum duorum fratrum sororem Helenam fuisse Trimalchio, fabulas perturbans, affirmat?
pairs.question_en: Of which two 'brothers' does Trimalchio, garbling the myths, declare Helen to have been the sister?
pairs.derivation: Trimalchio's famous mythological muddle introducing the Homeristae: Helen the sister of 'Diomedes and Ganymedes', seized by Agamemnon who palmed off a doe on Diana. Anchored to Trimalchio + named figures; two-name answer supported verbatim; the garbling itself is the celebrated point (the real brothers being Castor and Pollux).

pairs.source_text: Ceterum, quemadmodum di volunt, dominus in domo factus sum, et ecce cepi ipsimi cerebellum. Quid multa? coheredem me Caesari fecit, et accepi patrimonium laticlavium.
pairs.question: Cum quo Trimalchio a patrono suo coheres testamento factus est?
pairs.question_en: With whom was Trimalchio made co-heir in his patron's will?
pairs.derivation: Trimalchio's master made him co-heir with the emperor — 'coheredem me Caesari fecit' — the origin of his 'senatorial' fortune (patrimonium laticlavium). Anchored to Trimalchio; single answer supported verbatim. Naming Caesar co-heir was real Roman testamentary prudence.

pairs.source_text: Quidni? inquit Giton, etiam circumcide nos, ut Iudaei videamur, et pertunde aures, ut imitemur Arabes, et increta facies, ut suos Gallia cives putet.
pairs.question: Quo corporis signo Iudaei apud Petronium distingui dicuntur, cum Giton fugae consilia deridet?
pairs.question_en: By what bodily mark are the Jews said to be distinguished in Petronius, when Giton mocks the escape plans?
pairs.derivation: Giton's mock-disguise catalogue attests the shared ethnographic markers: circumcision for Jews, pierced ears for Arabs, chalked faces for Gauls. Anchored to the named peoples; single answer supported verbatim. Ethnic-custom knowledge every Roman carried.

pairs.source_text: Ibit ad aras, Sancte, tuas hircus, pecoris pater; ibit ad aras corniger et querulae fetus suis, hostia lactens.
pairs.question: Quam hostiam praecipuam Encolpius Priapo, si fortuna arrisisset, ad aras se daturum vovit?
pairs.question_en: What chief victim did Encolpius vow to bring to Priapus' altars, should fortune smile on him?
pairs.answer_en: A he-goat, father of the flock.
pairs.derivation: Encolpius' votive prayer to Priapus promises the god's canonical victim, the goat (with a suckling pig). Anchored to Priapus + Encolpius; short answer supported verbatim. The goat as Priapus' sacrifice is shared cult knowledge.

pairs.source_text: duae tabulae in utroque poste defixae, quarum altera, si bene memini, hoc habebat inscriptum: III ET PRIDIE KALENDAS IANVARIAS C. NOSTER FORAS CENAT, altera lunae cursum stellarumque septem imagines pictas; et qui dies boni quique incommodi essent, distinguente bulla notabantur.
pairs.question: Quid altera tabula in poste triclinii Trimalchionis defixa pictum habebat?
pairs.answer: Lunae cursum stellarumque septem imagines, distinctis bulla diebus bonis et incommodis.
pairs.question_en: What did the second tablet fixed on Trimalchio's dining-room doorpost display?
pairs.answer_en: The course of the moon and images of the seven stars (planets), with lucky and unlucky days marked by studs.
pairs.derivation: The household calendar-tablet: moon's course, the seven planets, and dies boni/incommodi marked with studs — Roman hemerology on display. Anchored to Trimalchio's triclinium; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Itaque proxime cum hoc titulo proscripsit: C. POMPEIVS DIOGENES EX KALENDIS IVLIIS CENACVLVM LOCAT; IPSE ENIM DOMVM EMIT.
pairs.question: Cur C. Pompeius Diogenes, ut titulus apud Petronium testatur, cenaculum suum ex kalendis Iuliis locabat?
pairs.question_en: Why, as the posted notice in Petronius attests, was C. Pompeius Diogenes letting his garret from the first of July?
pairs.answer_en: Because he had bought a house himself.
pairs.derivation: The freedman's triumphant to-let notice: garret available from 1 July — 'for he has bought a house.' Anchored to the named C. Pompeius Diogenes; the reason is quoted verbatim. Rental culture (cenacula, July moving day) plus freedman social climbing.

pairs.source_text: Sed quomodo dicunt — ego nihil scio, sed audivi — quom Incuboni pilleum rapuisset, et thesaurum invenit.
pairs.question: Quid, ut vulgo apud Petronium narratur, invenit qui Incuboni pilleum rapuit?
pairs.question_en: What, as the popular story in Petronius has it, did the man find who snatched the cap of an Incubo?
pairs.derivation: The folk-belief that seizing the cap of an Incubo (a treasure-guarding goblin) yields his treasure, told of a rich fellow freedman. Anchored to the named Incubo of Roman folklore; single answer supported verbatim. Shared superstition, criterion 8's core.

pairs.source_text: Eodem die: Mithridates servus in crucem actus est, quia Gai nostri genio male dixerat.
pairs.question: Quam ob causam Mithridates servus, ut in actis Trimalchionis recitatum est, in crucem actus est?
pairs.question_en: For what reason, as read out in Trimalchio's estate gazette, was the slave Mithridates crucified?
pairs.answer_en: Because he had cursed the genius of Gaius (Trimalchio).
pairs.derivation: From the estate acta: the slave Mithridates crucified for cursing his master's genius. Anchored to the named slave + Trimalchio; the reason is quoted verbatim. The cult of the master's genius (sworn by, not cursed) is central Roman household religion.

pairs.source_text: Puer autem lippus, sordidissimis dentibus, catellam nigram atque indecenter pinguem prasina involuebat fascia ... Scylax, canino scilicet usus ingenio, taeterrimo latratu triclinium implevit Margaritamque Croesi paene laceravit.
pairs.question: Quo nomine catella nigra Croesi, deliciarum Trimalchionis, vocabatur?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of the black lapdog belonging to Croesus, Trimalchio's pet boy?
pairs.derivation: The lapdog Margarita, wrapped by Croesus in a green ribbon and nearly torn apart by Scylax. Anchored to the named Croesus + Trimalchio's household; single-name answer supported verbatim. Pet-keeping culture of the Cena.

pairs.source_text: Desperatum valde ingeniosus est: idem sutor est, idem cocus, idem pistor, omnis Musae mancipium. Duo tamen vitia habet, quae si non haberet, esset omnium numerum: recutitus est et stertit. ... Illum emi trecentis denariis.
pairs.question: Quanti Habinnas servum illum omnis Musae mancipium, qui Vergilium tam acide cantaverat, emisse se dixit?
pairs.question_en: For how much did Habinnas say he had bought that jack-of-all-trades slave who had recited Vergil so sourly?
pairs.derivation: Habinnas' price for his multi-talented slave: 300 denarii. Anchored to the named Habinnas; single sum supported verbatim. Slave prices are hard cultural realia; the scene (a slave mangling Aeneid 5.1 with Atellane verses) is a famous set piece.

pairs.source_text: complorataque singularis exempli femina ab omnibus quintum iam diem sine alimento trahebat.
pairs.question: Quotum iam diem sine alimento matrona Ephesia in conditorio mariti lugens trahebat, cum miles eam invenit?
pairs.question_en: Which day without food was the matron of Ephesus dragging through, mourning in her husband's vault, when the soldier found her?
pairs.derivation: The widow's five-day fast in the tomb — the number fact of the celebrated tale. Anchored to the matron of Ephesus; single ordinal answer supported verbatim.
